segments.t: A KTPH000SerialKTPH001 connection opens a terminal on a serial port of this computer instead of a network host, like PuTTY's serial sessions: the console port of a router or switch, a microcontroller board, a modem or any device behind a USB-to-serial adapter. It is selectable as a protocol in both KTPH002Quick ConnectKTPH003 and the KTPH004Connection ManagerKTPH005 on Windows, macOS and Linux.

There is no login and no password prompt: what you type goes out on the line, and what the device sends is shown in the tab. Host, port, username and authentication are not used and are disabled in the dialogs.
Choose KTPH000SerialKTPH001 as the protocol, then fill in the serial rows below it.

The port to open: KTPH000 on Windows, KTPH001 or KTPH002 on Linux, KTPH003 on macOS. Pick it from the list or type it; a port that is not plugged in yet can be typed too. See KTPH004Finding the right portKTPH005.
300 to 921600 from the list, or any other rate typed in (up to 20000000). Default 9600.

5–8 data bits; KTPH000No parityKTPH001, KTPH002OddKTPH003, KTPH004EvenKTPH005, KTPH006MarkKTPH007 or KTPH008SpaceKTPH009; KTPH0101 stop bitKTPH011, KTPH0121.5 stop bitsKTPH013 or KTPH0142 stop bitsKTPH015. Default 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit (8N1).
KTPH001CRKTPH002 (default), KTPH003LFKTPH004 or KTPH005CR LFKTPH006: what the KTPH007KTPH000KTPH008 key is sent as, for devices that expect a line feed. Other keys are sent unchanged.

KTPH000Raise DTR on connectKTPH001 and KTPH002Raise RTS on connectKTPH003 (both on, as in PuTTY): some boards, Arduino among them, reset when DTR rises, so turn it off to keep them running. A flow-control mode that uses a line keeps it to itself, and its box is disabled. KTPH004Local echoKTPH005 shows what you type yourself, for devices that do not echo it back.

The settings are stored with the connection and survive duplicating, exporting and importing; picking a saved serial connection in Quick Connect shows them in the form. A connection without a name is called after its port and speed, for example KTPH000.

KTPH000Character encodingKTPH001 in the connection editor also applies to serial connections: KTPH002Use defaultKTPH003 follows KTPH004Settings → Terminal → EncodingKTPH005; many devices send plain ASCII or ISO-8859-1.

The list under KTPH002Serial port:KTPH003 shows every port of this computer with its driver's description, for example KTPH000, and below it what the USB adapter reports about itself: its manufacturer, its serial number (KTPH004S/NKTPH005) and its USB vendor and product id (KTPH006USB 0403:6001KTPH007); pointing at a port shows the USB location it is plugged into. The serial number tells two adapters of the same kind apart. On macOS each port appears once, as its KTPH001 device, which opens without waiting for a carrier signal.

While the dialog is open and KTPH000SerialKTPH001 is selected, korTTY looks for ports again every two seconds. A port that appears after the dialog opened is marked KTPH002NewKTPH003, and when no port is entered yet it is picked right away, so the simplest way to find an adapter is to plug it in with the dialog open. KTPH004RefreshKTPH005 looks again at once.

KTPH000Send BreakKTPH001 holds the line in the break condition for a quarter second, which drops a Cisco device into ROMMON or sends a Linux console's SysRq. It is in the terminal's context menu of a serial pane and in KTPH002Connections → Send BreakKTPH003 for the focused pane. The menu item has no key by default; give it one in KTPH004Settings → KeyboardKTPH005.

A serial line has no window size, so resizing the tab tells the device nothing. When the adapter is unplugged or its driver gives up, the tab stays open with the message KTPH000Serial port … disconnectedKTPH001 and the reconnect offer, as for a dropped network connection.
Closing a serial tab asks KTPH000Close the serial port?KTPH001 unless the connection may close without confirmation.

In the Connection Manager a serial connection shows a plug symbol, its port and line settings (KTPH000), and KTPH001Serial portKTPH002 and KTPH003LineKTPH004 in the inspector. SFTP, tunnels, the jump server, the host-key check, the AI Swarm and scheduled headless runs need a network host and are not offered for serial connections.

Serial sessions in a KTPH004MobaXtermKTPH005 session file (KTPH000, KTPH001) and a KTPH006PuTTY Connection ManagerKTPH007 CSV export are imported as serial connections with their port and speed; the other line settings start at 8N1 without flow control. From MobaXterm, a Windows port shown as KTPH002 becomes KTPH003.

Plug in the adapter with the dialog open and pick the port marked KTPH000NewKTPH001; USB adapters can get a different name after re-plugging. On Windows the Device Manager lists the port under KTPH002Ports (COM KTPH004 LPT)KTPH003.
KTPH000Serial port … is in use by another program.KTPH001
Close the other terminal program or tab that has the port open. korTTY opens a port exclusively.
KTPH000You may not open serial port ….KTPH001
On Linux, add your user to the KTPH000 group (KTPH001 on Arch Linux) and log in again.
The adapter does not support the speed; pick a standard rate.
The Flatpak package has device access (KTPH000), so serial ports under KTPH001 are visible inside the sandbox; the KTPH002 group membership on the host still applies.

An organization can forbid serial connections with KTPH000 in its KTPH001enterprise policyKTPH002. The connection editor and Quick Connect then no longer offer KTPH003SerialKTPH004 for new connections, and opening a saved or imported serial connection is refused with KTPH005Your organization's policy does not allow serial connections.KTPH006 The server allowlist of the policy does not apply to serial ports, as they have no host.
A serial session runs inside korTTY itself. It cannot be KTPH000isolatedKTPH001 in a process or sandbox of its own; when your organization requires isolation, korTTY does not open the port.
